title: Eliminating Old Karma
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Answer: In the Dream Journey Collection, “Instruction to Dong Zhiguang,” Master Hanshan teaches:

inline.s: The great sea of all karmic hindrances arises entirely from deluded thought.
If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate true suchness.
The many sins are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can melt away.
Question: How does one eliminate old karma?
Answer: In his Dream Journey Collection
Instruction to Dong Zhiguang
, Master Hanshan teaches:

[An ancient worthy taught people: “At all times eliminate old karma, and by no means create new misfortune.” For sentient beings whose karma is heavy, the Buddha opened the single gate of repentance, which is the most direct expedient for leaving suffering behind. A verse says: “The many sins are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can melt away; if one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate true suchness.” This is the principal practice; apart from this, all else is auxiliary expedient.]

An ancient worthy taught people: “At all times eliminate old karma, and by no means create new misfortune.” For sentient beings whose karma is heavy, the single gate of repentance taught by the Buddha is the most direct expedient for leaving suffering behind. A verse says: “The many sins are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can melt away; if one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate true suchness” (later the text says: “the mind that has nothing in it is true suchness”). This is the principal practice; apart from this, all else is auxiliary practice.

[The many sins are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can melt away] Just as the sun melts frost and dew, so contemplating true suchness (the sun of wisdom) can eliminate the many sins. The Sutra on the Contemplation of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra says:

“The great sea of all karmic hindrances arises entirely from deluded thought. If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate true suchness. The many sins are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can melt away.”
[Sea of karmic hindrances] karmic hindrances as deep and vast as a great sea. [Sit upright and contemplate true suchness] Later the text says:
“The mind that has nothing in it is true suchness.”

[The self-nature of sentient beings is equal to that of the Buddhas; it is originally undefiled, and has no mark of birth and death or coming and going. Only because of the first non-awakening, being deluded as to one’s own self-nature, is it called ignorance. Because of ignorance, various deluded thoughts arise, with all manner of inversion, and various kinds of karma are created, and one falsely seizes the suffering of birth and death in the three realms. All of this is ignorance, failing to understand one’s own mind and being turned about by deluded thoughts. It is like a person in deep sleep who dreams many bad dreams, with all kinds of scenes and all kinds of terror, suffering unbearably. When he wakes, he seeks the events of the dream and finds them utterly unobtainable. Thus sentient beings, fallen into the dream of ignorance, follow deluded thoughts in inversion, create various kinds of karma, and bring suffering upon themselves. Seen with awakened eyes, how could these inverted states be obtained at all?]

The self-nature of sentient beings is equal to that of the Buddhas; it is originally undefiled, and has no mark of birth and death or coming and going. But because of the first non-awakening, being deluded as to one’s own self-nature (entering the dream of ignorance), this is ignorance. Because of ignorance, all deluded thoughts arise, and so all manner of inversion arises, and various kinds of karma are created, and one falsely seizes the suffering of birth and death in the three realms. All of this is ignorance — failing to understand one’s own mind and being pulled about by deluded thoughts. It is like a person in deep sleep who dreams many bad dreams, with all kinds of scenes and all kinds of terror, suffering unbearably. When he wakes, he seeks the events of the dream and finds them utterly unobtainable. So too sentient beings, fallen into the dream of ignorance, follow deluded thoughts in inversion, create various kinds of karma, and bring suffering upon themselves. Seen with awakened eyes, where are these inverted states at all?

[Now, right within the dream of ignorance at present, how can one manage to eliminate old karma? One must use the light of wisdom to shine through and break apart ignorance, and firmly believe that one’s own mind is originally pure and is not to be commanded by deluded thoughts and inversions. Then the various karmas have no cause, for deluded thought is the cause of the various karmas. Why is this? Because from time without beginning we have been deluded as to our own fundamental mind, and life after life, age after age, have created various karmas with the deluded mind. These karmic habits accumulate within the field of the eighth consciousness, watered by the water of ignorance, causing these evil seeds to send forth karmic sprouts — this is the root of sin, from which all evil karma arises.]

Now then, already within the dream of ignorance at present, how can one eliminate old karma? One must use the light of wisdom to shine through and break apart ignorance, and firmly believe that one’s own mind is originally pure and is not to be driven by deluded thoughts and inversions. In this way there is no cause for creating karma, for deluded thought is the cause of the various karmas. Why is this? Because from time without beginning we have been deluded as to our own fundamental mind, and life after life, age after age, have created various karmas with the deluded mind. These karmic habits accumulate within the ālaya consciousness (the eighth consciousness), watered by the water of ignorance, causing these evil seeds to send forth karmic sprouts — this is the root of sin, from which all evil karma arises.

[If one now wishes old karma to be eliminated, one must first bring forth the great light of wisdom, shine through and break apart ignorance, and not allow deluded thought to sprout and grow secretly in the dark. If at the very place where deluded thought arises one can cut it off with a single thought, then the karmic roots accumulated of old are eliminated on the spot. This is what is meant by “do not fear the arising of thoughts, only fear the lateness of awakening.” If one’s illuminating awareness is the least bit late, one is turned about by it. If, in the place where thoughts arise and move in daily life, one can be aware of each thought and dissolve each thought, this is “the many sins are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can melt away.” For the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom — this is what is meant by wisdom being able to eliminate.]

If one now wishes to eliminate old karma, one must first bring forth the great light of wisdom, shine through and break apart ignorance, and not allow deluded thought to sprout and grow secretly in the dark. If at the very place where deluded thought arises one can cut it off with a single thought (a sudden, awe-struck awakening), then the karmic roots accumulated of old are eliminated on the spot. This is what is meant by ‘do not fear the arising of thoughts, only fear the lateness of awakening.’ If one’s illuminating awareness is the least bit late, one is turned about by it (the deluded thought). If, in the place where thoughts arise and move in daily life, one can be aware of each thought and dissolve each thought, this is “the many sins are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can melt away.” For the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom — this is wisdom being able to eliminate the many sins.

[If, day and night without letup, you diligently observe and never let it pass, and at the very place where deluded thought arises thoroughly investigate it, you will find there is no mark of arising at all. Look and look again, and ultimately it is unobtainable. After long practice and full familiarity, your own mind will be pure and without anything in it, and the mind that has nothing in it is true suchness. If you constantly contemplate this mind, what deluded thought could be harbored there, and what accumulated karma could lodge there? To apply the mind in this way is called the samādhi of illuminating contemplation.]

You must, day and night without letup, diligently observe and never let it pass; and at the very place where deluded thought arises, thoroughly investigate it, and you will find there is no mark of arising at all. Look and look again, and ultimately the deluded thought is utterly unobtainable. After long practice and full familiarity, your own mind will be pure and without anything in it, and the mind that has nothing in it is true suchness. If you constantly contemplate this pure mind, what deluded thought could be harbored there, and what accumulated karma could lodge there? To apply the mind in this way is called the samādhi of illuminating contemplation.

[If, day and night without letup, you diligently observe] Here “ruò” means you. For example: “If I changed your service and restored your taxes, what then?” (This line comes from Liu Zongyuan’s The Snake Catcher; translation: If I changed your service of catching poisonous snakes and restored your taxes, what would you think?)
